o: Explain the overall purpose of the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
Recognise unauthorised access and unauthorised harmful acts.
Apply the legislation accurately to short scenarios.
c: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes certain actions against computer systems unlawful, including access without permission.
Accessing computer material without authorisation can be an offence, even if the person does not steal information. Knowing a password does not by itself grant permission.
Unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate another offence is a more serious form of computer misuse.

Unauthorised acts that impair a system—such as deliberately causing harmful disruption or altering data without permission—can be offences. Authorised security testing must stay within a lawful agreed scope.

m.title: Permission matters even without changes
m.q: A student guesses a teacher's password and opens restricted files without permission, but changes nothing. Explain why this may be an offence under the Computer Misuse Act 1990. [4 marks]
st: Identify the action: deliberately accessing another person's account.
The student gains access to computer material [1] without permission [1].
The Computer Misuse Act covers unauthorised access [1] even if no data is modified or deleted [1].
Do not incorrectly claim that a file must be damaged before unauthorised access becomes unlawful.

w: An employee opens confidential HR records using a colleague's password without permission. Explain why knowing the password does not make the access lawful. [4 marks]
The employee uses an account to access restricted computer records [1] without being authorised [1]. Knowing a password is not permission [1], so the access may breach the Computer Misuse Act [1].
A person deliberately changes a shared database so the service stops working. Explain which kind of computer misuse is involved and one effect. [4 marks]
The changes were unauthorised [1] and impair the operation of the system [1]. This can amount to a Computer Misuse Act offence [1], and legitimate users may be unable to access the service/data [1].
A school hires an expert to test its website security. Explain TWO reasons written permission and a defined scope are important. [4 marks]

Permission shows the tester is authorised [1] and distinguishes the agreed test from unauthorised access [1]. A defined scope identifies permitted systems and actions [1], preventing the tester from exceeding authorisation [1].

k.q: Simulate a basic permission check. This example is not a real authentication system.
k.code:
allowed = 0
if allowed == 1 then
    print("Access permitted")
else
    print("Ask for authorisation")
endif
p: Add print("Check the permitted scope") after the IF statement.
k.a:
When allowed = 0: Ask for authorisation. With allowed = 1: Access permitted.

Extended OCR ERL:
allowed = 1
if allowed == 1 then
    print("Access permitted")
else
    print("Ask for authorisation")
endif
print("Check the permitted scope")

Only a teaching simulation; real permission must come from the system owner.

A pupil opens another pupil's school account without permission but does not delete any work. Explain why this can still be computer misuse. [4 marks]

Source: Original OCR J277-style teaching question; not an official OCR past paper.
The account contains computer material [1], which the pupil deliberately accessed [1] without permission [1]. Unauthorised access is prohibited even without deleting or modifying data [1].

Compare unauthorised access, access with further criminal intent, and unauthorised damage/disruption under the Computer Misuse Act. [6 marks]

Source: Original OCR J277-style teaching question; not an official OCR past paper.

Unauthorised access is entering computer material without permission [2]. Access with intent to commit another offence adds criminal purpose [2]. Deliberate unauthorised acts impairing systems/data can disrupt operation [2]. Apply examples accurately without assuming legitimate security testing is unlawful.

Entering or using computer material without permission.
Permission to access or use a system.

Damage or disruption to computer operation or data.
x: Accessing someone else's account without permission can be unlawful even if no files are deleted.
r: State the overall purpose of the Data Protection Act 2018. [2 marks]
Regulates/protects the processing of personal data [1] and helps protect people's privacy/information rights [1].
State TWO environmental concerns linked to digital technology. [2 marks]
E-waste from discarded devices [1] and electricity/energy consumption [1]. Other clear valid concerns include manufacturing emissions or extracting raw materials.
Using 1 KB = 1,000 bytes, convert 3 KB to bytes. [1 mark]
A secondary school moves all homework online. Explain one benefit and one social disadvantage. [4 marks]

Homework can be accessed anywhere with Internet [1], making resources easy to distribute/submit [1]. Pupils without reliable devices or connectivity [1] may find it harder to complete work, widening inequality [1].

priorExam.q: A school app requests pupils' names, emergency contacts and favourite music. Explain TWO data-protection responsibilities when collecting this information. [4 marks]
priorExam.a: Identify and communicate a lawful, specific purpose [1], so people know why data is collected [1]. Minimise personal information collected [1], avoiding unnecessary items such as favourite music [1].
